content: Neonatal sepsis refers to a bloodstream infection occurring in infants younger than 90 days of age. It is categorized into two types: early-onset sepsis, which occurs within the first week of life, and late-onset sepsis, which develops between days 8 and 89 of life. Symptoms of Neonatal Sepsis: Infants with neonatal sepsis may present with the following clinical signs: Alterations in body temperature, either fever or hypothermia. Respiratory difficulties, such as rapid breathing or apnea. Episodes of diarrhea. Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar levels). Decreased physical activity or lethargy. Poor feeding or reduced sucking reflex. Seizures or convulsions. Bradycardia (abnormally slow heart rate). Abdominal distension or a swollen belly. Vomiting. Jaundice, characterized by yellowing of the skin and the whites of the eyes. Causes of Neonatal Sepsis: Neonatal sepsis is commonly caused by bacterial pathogens such as Escherichia coli, Listeria monocytogenes, and certain strains of Streptococcus (e.g., Group B Streptococcus). Early-onset neonatal sepsis typically manifests within the first 24 hours after birth. The infection is often transmitted from the mother to the infant either before or during delivery. Risk factors for early-onset sepsis include: Maternal Group B Streptococcus infection during pregnancy. Preterm delivery. Prolonged rupture of membranes (lasting more than 24 hours before delivery). Maternal chorioamnionitis (infection of the placental tissues and amniotic fluid). Late-onset neonatal sepsis occurs after delivery and is often acquired from the environment. Risk factors include: Prolonged use of intravenous catheters. Extended hospital stays. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care: Immediate medical attention is required if an infant exhibits any symptoms of neonatal sepsis. Diagnosis: The diagnosis of neonatal sepsis involves laboratory testing to confirm the presence of infection and identify the causative organism. Diagnostic procedures may include: Blood tests, such as: Blood culture to detect bacterial growth. C-reactive protein (CRP) levels to assess inflammation. Complete blood count (CBC) to evaluate white blood cell levels. Lumbar puncture (spinal tap) to analyze cerebrospinal fluid for bacterial infection. Chest X-ray if the infant has respiratory symptoms, such as coughing or difficulty breathing. Urine culture in infants older than a few days to check for urinary tract infections. Treatment Options: Infants hospitalized for suspected sepsis, particularly those younger than 4 weeks, are started on broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately, even before laboratory results are available. This approach, which may take 24–72 hours for confirmation, has been life-saving in many cases. Older infants may not require antibiotics if all laboratory results are normal. In such cases, close outpatient monitoring is recommended. Infants requiring treatment are admitted to the hospital for continuous monitoring and care. Prognosis: With prompt and appropriate treatment, many infants with bacterial infections recover fully without long-term complications. However, neonatal sepsis remains a leading cause of infant mortality. Early intervention significantly improves outcomes. Potential Complications: Long-term disabilities. Death. Prevention: Preventive measures include: Administering prophylactic antibiotics to pregnant women with risk factors such as chorioamnionitis, Group B Streptococcus colonization, or a history of delivering an infant with sepsis caused by these bacteria. Treating maternal infections promptly and ensuring a clean birthing environment. Delivering the baby within 24 hours of membrane rupture, when feasible, to reduce the risk of infection.
